newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Hundreds leap off 400m peak in NZ for bungy thrill.
newsitem.headline: Hundreds leap off 400m peak in NZ for bungy thrill.

text.p: New Zealand's reputation as a thrill-seeker's paradise took a huge plunge on Sunday with the launch of a scary new bungy jump in the country's adventure tourism capital, Queenstown.

Hundreds queued to throw themselves screaming from "The Ledge", built off a peak 400 metres (1,300 feet) above the picturesque township in New Zealand's South Island, with only a rubber cord tied to their feet.

Jumpers actually plunge some 30 metres (100 feet) before the cord reaches the limits of its elasticity and flings them back up again. But the thrill is heightened by a sheer cliff face on one side and a view of Queenstown directly below.
Participants are rescued when the yo-yoing finally stops.
"It's absolutely awesome," gasped one woman after taking the death-defying plunge.
The jump is a creation of bungy pioneers AJ Hackett Bungy, whose co-founder A.J. Hackett made world headlines in 1987 when he leapt from the Eiffel Tower in Paris.
The company operates two more bungy jumps in Queenstown and another five overseas.
"It's not for the faint-hearted, but it's extremely safe and everyone who's brave enough to try it loves it," Managing Director Henry van Asch said.

Queenstown, which attracts about 650,000 visitors a year including 450,000 from overseas, is currently hosting the southern hemisphere's biggest winter festival. Tourism is New Zealand's single largest export earner.
Commercial bungy jumping has its origins in an ancient tradition found on the tiny island of Pentecost in the South Pacific Vanuatu group.

For hundreds of years, men from Pentecost have climbed to the top of 35-metre (115 feet) towers, tied vines to their feet and flung themselves at the ground. Manhood is put to the test and a good yam harvest is assured.
